summary: This proposed standard defines an initial set of textual conventions, reusable data types, available to all SNMPv2 MIB modules. It was replaced by RFC 1903.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of redescribing common things like an address every time, this paper defines shared names for them that everyone can reuse.

questions: reusable data types in mib modules
subtitle: Standard reusable data types for network management specifications.

tldr.problem: Network management systems need to describe many managed objects, and writers of MIB modules keep defining the same data types over and over, like MAC addresses or time intervals, each with slightly different semantics and documentation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1443 defines the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro and an initial set of textual conventions - reusable named data types with standardized semantics - so that MIB modules can declare objects using a common vocabulary instead of defining basic types repeatedly.
tldr.outcome: This became the foundation for SNMP management information. The textual conventions defined here (like RowStatus, DisplayString, and DateAndTime) are used in virtually all SNMPv2 and later MIBs. It was superseded by RFC 1903 which refined and expanded the set.

facts.label: Textual conventions defined
facts.value: 13 core types including DisplayString, MacAddress, RowStatus, TimeStamp

today: RFC 1443 was obsoleted by RFC 1903, which refined the macro definition and added more textual conventions (Counter64, Bits, etc.). However, the core conventions from RFC 1443 remain foundational to SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 MIB design. Most network devices use RowStatus for table management, DisplayString for text, and the other conventions for standard semantic types across the industry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A network management system monitors and controls devices (routers, switches, servers) by reading and writing management information stored in each device's Management Information Base (MIB). The MIB is a virtual database of managed objects, described using the Structure of Management Information (SMI), a subset of ASN.1 notation.

When MIB modules are written, they need to define the data types of each managed object. Many of these types are conceptually simple but appear repeatedly: a MAC address, a text string, a time value, a yes/no flag, or the status of a network table entry. Rather than define the same basic types in isolation, RFC 1443 defines textual conventions (named, standardized data types with shared semantics) that MIB writers can reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB describes objects in a network device. Many objects use common types like addresses or times. Instead of describing them separately each time, this memo creates standard definitions everyone can reuse.

sections.title: What Textual Conventions Are
sections.content:
A textual convention is a named data type with an underlying primitive syntax (like INTEGER or OCTET STRING) plus additional semantics and display hints. For example, DisplayString is an OCTET STRING of at most 255 characters that holds NVT ASCII text; MacAddress is an OCTET STRING of exactly 6 bytes representing an 802 MAC address; TruthValue is an INTEGER with values 1 (true) and 2 (false).

Each convention is defined using a TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro that specifies a name, a status (current, deprecated, or obsolete), a description, an optional DISPLAY-HINT for how to format the value, and the underlying SYNTAX. Objects defined using a textual convention are encoded using the rules of their underlying type, but tools and humans understand them according to the convention's semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: A textual convention is like a label that says this is a MAC address or this is a true/false value. It uses a basic data type underneath but adds special meaning.

sections.title: Core Textual Conventions
sections.content:
RFC 1443 defines thirteen textual conventions covering common patterns. DisplayString represents text strings up to 255 characters. PhysAddress and MacAddress represent physical addresses; MacAddress specifically follows IEEE 802 conventions with a fixed 6-byte size. TruthValue is a boolean (1 for true, 2 for false). TimeStamp is the system uptime when an event occurred, and TimeInterval represents a duration in units of 0.01 seconds.

DateAndTime encodes a full date, time, and timezone in 8 or 11 octets. TestAndIncr is an integer used for atomic test-and-increment operations. AutonomousType identifies an object identifier for extensible types. InstancePointer points to a specific instance in a MIB table. RowStatus manages table rows with values for creation, activation, and deletion of conceptual rows.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo defines types for common things like text strings, addresses, times, dates, booleans, and table management. Each one has a standard name and meaning.

sections.title: RowStatus and Table Management
sections.content:
RowStatus is the most complex textual convention. It manages the creation and deletion of rows in a conceptual MIB table. A row status column has six possible values: active (row is in use), notInService (row exists but is disabled), notReady (row exists but lacks required information), createAndGo (create and activate in one step), createAndWait (create but leave inactive), and destroy (delete the row).

The RFC includes a detailed state diagram and interaction sequence for how management stations use these values to create, initialize, suspend, and delete table rows. This protocol handles the complexity of creating a table entry with multiple columns, some of which may have defaults and some of which may be required. The protocol prevents partial rows from consuming resources indefinitely by requiring agents to delete rows left in intermediate states for more than five minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: RowStatus is like the instructions for adding, editing, and removing entries from a table. It has values for create, activate, pause, and delete.

sections.title: The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION Macro and Mapping Rules
sections.content:
A textual convention is formally defined using the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro, which specifies five clauses. The DISPLAY-HINT clause (optional) tells tools how to format the value for display: for integers, use 'x' for hex, 'd' for decimal, 'o' for octal, 'b' for binary; for octet strings, use format specs like '1x:' (one byte as hex with colon separator) or '255a' (up to 255 bytes as ASCII).

The STATUS clause indicates whether the definition is current, deprecated, or obsolete. The DESCRIPTION clause explains the semantics. The REFERENCE clause (optional) cites related specifications. The SYNTAX clause (required) specifies the underlying data type and any constraints. ASN.1 subtypes are allowed on most types to add range or size limits, except for Counter types.
sections.plainLanguage: The macro is a template for defining new types. It has slots for a name, status, description, display hints, and the underlying data type.
